lessons.title: Datums and the datum reference frame
explanation: A loose part can slide along and rotate about X, Y and Z, which makes six degrees of freedom. Datums lock these down so the part can be measured in a known coordinate system.
A datum feature is a real surface on the part, such as a face or a hole. The datum is the perfect, theoretical plane, axis or point that comes from it.
The datum feature symbol, a boxed letter joined to a triangle on the surface, tells you which surface is which datum.
In a feature control frame, datum letters are listed in order of precedence: primary, secondary, tertiary. Together they form the datum reference frame.
lessons.diagramAlt: A block whose uneven bottom surface is datum feature A, resting on a perfect dashed datum plane. Datum feature B is the left side.
lessons.commonMistake: Treating datum order as unimportant. A | B | C and A | C | B are different reference frames. The primary datum is set first, and later datums cannot change what earlier ones already fixed.
lessons.sources: Berez, Fundamentals of GD&T Part I, slides 16 to 22. NASA GD and T Basics, slides 16 and 18.

quiz.question: How many degrees of freedom does a free rigid part have?
quiz.explanation: Three translations along X, Y and Z, plus three rotations about them: six in total.

quiz.question: A frame ends with | A | B | C |. Which datum is primary?
options: None. The order does not matter.
quiz.explanation: Datums are listed in order of precedence, so the first letter, A, is primary.

lessons.title: Flatness
explanation: Flatness is a form control. It limits how far a single surface may stray from a perfect plane.
Its tolerance zone is two parallel planes spaced the tolerance value apart, and every point of the surface must lie between them.
Flatness compares the surface only with itself. It never references a datum, and its zone is free to float to wherever the surface fits.
It is a good choice for faces that mate, seal or carry load.
lessons.diagramAlt: A block with a wavy top surface sitting inside two dashed parallel lines 0.05 apart, with a flatness frame pointing at the top.
lessons.commonMistake: Confusing flatness with parallelism. Parallelism controls a surface relative to a datum. Flatness has no datum at all, so a datum letter in a flatness frame is an error.
lessons.sources: Berez, Fundamentals of GD&T Part I, slides 27, 30 and 34. NASA GD and T Basics, slide 22.

quiz.question: What is the shape of a flatness tolerance zone?
quiz.explanation: The surface must fit between two parallel planes spaced the tolerance value apart.

quiz.question: Which datum does a flatness frame reference?
options: The primary datum of the part
Any datum on the opposite face
quiz.explanation: Flatness is a form control. It compares the surface only with itself, so it takes no datum.

lessons.title: Perpendicularity
explanation: Perpendicularity is an orientation control. It limits how far a surface or an axis may stray from exactly 90° to a datum.
Because it is measured relative to something, a perpendicularity frame always names at least one datum.
For a flat surface, the zone is two parallel planes the tolerance value apart, standing at 90° to the datum. In a 2D view they appear as two parallel lines.
For the axis of a hole or pin, the zone can instead be a cylinder.
lessons.diagramAlt: A block on datum A whose slightly tilted right face sits inside two dashed vertical lines 0.1 apart.
lessons.commonMistake: Leaving the datum out. Without a datum there is nothing to be perpendicular to, so the frame is incomplete.
lessons.sources: Berez, Fundamentals of GD&T Part I, slides 27, 32 and 33. NASA GD and T Basics, slide 25.

quiz.question: Perpendicularity belongs to which group of controls?
quiz.explanation: Perpendicularity, parallelism and angularity are the orientation controls.

quiz.question: For a flat surface, what is the perpendicularity tolerance zone?
options: Two parallel planes at 90° to the datum
Two planes parallel to the datum
quiz.explanation: The zone is two parallel planes the tolerance value apart, standing at 90° to the datum.

lessons.title: Position
explanation: Position is a location control. It limits how far the center, axis or center plane of a feature of size, such as a hole, may wander from its true position.
The true position is set by basic dimensions. These are exact numbers drawn in a box, and they carry no tolerance of their own.
A diameter symbol (Ø) before the tolerance makes the zone a cylinder, which looks like a circle in a top view. The real axis must stay inside it.
Position always references datums, which say where the measurement starts.
lessons.diagramAlt: A plate with a hole located by boxed basic dimensions 30 and 20 from datums B and C, a position frame, and a magnified circular zone.
lessons.commonMistake: Locating a hole with ± dimensions while also giving it a position tolerance. Position needs basic (boxed) dimensions to define the true position.
lessons.sources: Berez, Fundamentals of GD&T Part I, slides 27, 28, 35 and 43. NASA GD and T Basics, slides 16 and 23.

quiz.question: What defines the true position of a hole?
quiz.explanation: Basic dimensions are exact and locate the center of the position tolerance zone.

quiz.question: In a position frame, what does Ø0.2 describe?
options: A cylindrical zone 0.2 mm in diameter
The hole is 0.2 mm in diameter
The hole may be 0.2 mm larger
quiz.explanation: The Ø makes the zone a cylinder, and 0.2 is its diameter. The hole's axis must stay inside it.
